_README: Model-generated review findings for machine-translated strings. These are MODEL judgments, NOT native-speaker judgments — they are a prioritized worklist for a human reviewer, not a set of approved corrections. Nothing here has been applied except objective script-corruption repairs (see applied[]).
reviewer: claude subagent per language, 424 highest-stakes strings each (safety/pain/help/refusal/body + core words + UI chrome)

applied.why: Latin word embedded in Ge'ez — objectively broken
Arabic ط substituted for Ge'ez ጥ

findings.issue: ቁም is intransitive 'stand still' (addressee stops their own motion); it does not convey 'stop doing that to me', the refusal/protest sense 'Stop' carries as a core AAC safety word. A user trying to stop unwanted touching or an action against them may not be understood.
Same core-safety word as cw-stop; ቁም means 'stand still', not the transitive 'cease doing that (to me)' sense needed for a refusal/protest button.
Same issue as cw-stop/help-stop: intransitive 'stand still' instead of the transitive refusal sense 'stop that'.

This means 'I am not pleased/happy' (emotional), not 'I do not feel well' (physical wellness). In a help-needs list next to symptom words, this flip could cause a caregiver to read the child as unhappy rather than physically unwell, delaying appropriate response.

አንገላታኝ means 'it troubled/mistreated/harassed me', not dizziness. A genuine medical symptom (dizziness, which can precede fainting) is replaced with an unrelated and alarming concept (being mistreated). Compare hb-dizzy-spell, which correctly uses ማዞር.
This means 'I am trembling/shaking', not dizzy. Same symptom-word error as help-i-feel-dizzy, with a different wrong word — the corpus has two inconsistent, both-wrong translations of 'dizzy'.

Corrupted string: contains a bare Latin word 'his' embedded mid-sentence in Ge'ez text, and the remaining text is not coherent Amharic ('what does ... do'). This will mispronounce or fail in TTS and does not mean 'You're welcome'.
Contains an Arabic letter ط (not Ge'ez) in place of ጥ — a script violation on a health/body word. This will break or mispronounce in TTS.
Corrupted text: a stray, disconnected 'እ' character precedes the sentence, likely a generation artifact. Will be spoken as garbage/mispronounced.
Same corruption as help-i-am-sleepy: stray disconnected 'እ' before the sentence.

ደውልላት is the benefactive 'call [it] for her' (3rd person feminine), not 'call my mom [for me]'. The pronoun agreement is wrong — it tells the listener to phone on behalf of some other 'her', not the speaker. Safety-relevant because this tile is used to summon help.
ደውልለት is benefactive 'call [it] for him' (3rd masc), wrong agreement for a first-person request to phone one's own father. Same class of error as help-call-my-mom.

አስቦኛል means roughly 'it occurred to me / made me think', not 'worried'. The correct anxious/worried sense (ተጨንቄአለሁ) is already used correctly for the adjacent 'Anxious' and 'Stressed' tiles, making this one an outlier wrong-sense error for a closely related feeling.

ተው actually means 'Stop it / leave it / don't' (imperative of 'to abandon'), which is nearly the opposite sense of permissive 'Let' (as in 'let me...'). This is a foundational core word combined into many generated sentences, so the error propagates. Note qt-never-mind also correctly uses ተው for its own (different) meaning, confirming ተው is not 'let'.

አዛን is not a standard, grammatically complete Amharic word (neither a valid adjective nor a conjugated verb) — it reads as incomplete/garbled. 'Sad' is a foundational emotion word for an AAC device and this entry is unusable as spoken output.

ተቀመጥ specifically means 'Sit down', a different physical instruction than 'Stay' (remain in place, regardless of standing/sitting). Mixing up a mobility instruction like this can cause real confusion about what is being asked.
መላላት means 'to become loose/slack', unrelated to a bruise. This is an inaccurate medical/body-injury term.
ደንግዟል is from 'to be startled/shocked/dazed', not the loss-of-sensation meaning of 'numb'. Body-sensation word mismatch.
This is identical to the translation used for fe-itchy ('it itches me'), collapsing two distinct sensations (itchy vs. ticklish) into one, which is the wrong sense for 'ticklish'.

ተረብሻለሁ means 'I am disturbed/upset/agitated', not 'confused'. The corpus already has the correct word for confused (ግራ ተጋብቻለሁ) at fe-confused, making this an inconsistent wrong-sense pick for the same concept.

ነርሷን carries a 3rd-person-feminine possessive ('her nurse'), not the intended generic/definite 'the nurse'. Adds a confusing, unintended possessive relationship on a safety-relevant call-for-help tile.
ባታሪው means 'the battery' (definite article), dropping the possessive 'my'. Ambiguous whose battery is being reported dead on a device the user relies on to communicate.

ማቀፍ is the infinitive/gerund 'to hug/embrace' with no indication of direction; as phrased this can read as 'I want to hug [someone]' rather than 'I want to be hugged'. Ambiguous agency on a needs/comfort request.
ሒዘኝ is not a standard Amharic verb form (likely a corrupted/misspelled form of 'ያዘኝ'/'ያዝልኝ'). Will be mispronounced or fail to convey the request.
Likely misspelled imperative-plus-object; the standard form combining the imperative 'እይ' (watch/see) with the object suffix '-ኝ' (me) is 'እይኝ', not 'እየኝ'.
Literal, non-idiomatic calque ('at one time, one') that is not how a spoken Amharic request for turn-taking is phrased; a listener may not parse it as 'one at a time'.
This is only the bare noun 'break/rest', dropping the verb — it says 'Break', not the actionable request 'Take a break'. Compare help-i-need-a-break, which correctly phrases the full request.

This is identical to how literal physical cold would be phrased (same as help-i-am-cold's meaning), losing the metaphorical/emotional 'inside' distinction. A caregiver may think the user is physically cold and needs a blanket rather than emotionally distressed.
ረዳት is the noun 'helper/assistant', not the adjective 'helpful' — this duplicates pp-helper ('Helper') exactly, losing the distinct descriptive sense of 'Helpful'.
This is a relative-clause fragment ('...who is loved') that needs a following head noun; used standalone as a feeling-word it is grammatically incomplete.

Literally 'pleasant evening', which reads as 'Good evening' rather than the sleep-time farewell 'Good night'. Inconsistent with qt-good-night, which correctly uses ደህና እደር for the same English string.

This is plain 'Now', identical to how 'Now' alone would be said, dropping the urgency/emphasis 'Right' adds. Inconsistent with ti-right-now, which correctly uses the emphatic አሁኑኑ for the same English phrase.
Missing the emphatic/agreement marker ም that standard Amharic 'everyone' takes (ሁሉም ሰው); as written it reads as an unnatural 'all person'.
Spelling typo: should be ይመስለኛል ('it seems to me'); as written the vowel is wrong.

Missing reflexive '-ji-' morpheme. 'Sikia' without 'ji' means 'hear/perceive', so as written this reads as 'I hear badly' (a hearing complaint), not 'I feel sick'. Compare correctly-formed siblings 'Najisikia vizuri' and 'Sijisikii vizuri' elsewhere in this same file.

'Magonjwa' is the plural noun 'diseases/illnesses', not the adjective 'sick'. A user tapping this to say how they feel would instead announce 'diseases'. Correct sibling entry 'hfs-sick' already uses the right word ('Mgonjwa'), confirming this one is wrong.
Not a Swahili word; unintelligible. The correct word for knee is 'Goti'. A user pointing to knee pain would be unable to communicate the location at all.
Not a Swahili word (letter substitution). The correct medical term for injection/shot is 'Sindano'. Garbled medical vocabulary.
Not a recognized Swahili word for a wound/cut. Correct terms are 'Jeraha' (wound) or 'Mkato'. A user reporting an injury with this word would not be understood.
'Pasi' means a clothes iron (or a pass/permit) in Swahili — completely unrelated to 'bruise'. Wrong-sense mistranslation on a medical/injury word.

'Mbali' means 'far/distant', so this literally reads as 'pain that is far away', not 'dull pain'. Pain-character words are safety-critical for a caregiver or clinician triaging the complaint (sharp vs. dull matters medically); this materially miscommunicates.

Malformed verb — missing the present-tense subject prefix vowel. Should be 'Naogopa' (ni-na-ogopa contracted). 'Nogopa' is not a standard word and would sound wrong/unclear spoken aloud for a fear/safety disclosure.

'Kutega macho' is not the standard idiom for 'watch me' (kutega means to set a trap/lie in wait). This is a help-needs/safety-adjacent request (e.g. near stairs or water) and the non-standard phrasing risks not being understood as a supervision request.
'Sasa' means 'now', not 'Hi'. Spoken out of context by a non-speaking user this would sound like a non-sequitur ('Now.') rather than a greeting, and could confuse the listener.
'Eti' means 'so-called/allegedly' (used to express doubt or reported speech), not a greeting. Clear mistranslation of a core social-opener word.
Garbled/non-word — not real Swahili. Correct phrase is 'Heri ya kuzaliwa'. TTS would speak gibberish on a socially important phrase.
Garbled/non-word — missing syllables from 'jivunia'. Correct form is 'Ninakujivunia'.

'Amani moyoni' means 'peace in the heart', not 'warm inside' — wrong sense entirely. The parallel entry 'fe-cold-inside' correctly uses 'Baridi moyoni' (cold-in-heart), proving the intended pattern; this one breaks it.
Likely typo for 'Kifundo cha mkono'. 'Kipundo' is not standard. The correctly-formed sibling entry 'hb-ankle' ('Kifundo cha mguu') confirms the intended pattern and that this one is wrong.
Not a Swahili word. The correct term is 'Kisigino'.
'Inua kichwa' means 'raise/lift the head' — the wrong action (and roughly opposite motion) for a nod. As an action-vocabulary/instruction word this would teach or trigger the wrong physical gesture.
Not a standalone Swahili word — looks like a truncated fragment of '-mbie' (as in 'Niambie' = tell me). The correct core-verb citation form is 'Ambia'.

'Ili' means 'in order to/so that' (a conjunction) — a completely different word class from the pronoun 'It'. Since this is a composable core word meant to combine with other tiles, this substitution can produce nonsensical output sentences.

'Mimi' means 'I/me' (subject/object pronoun), not the possessive 'my'. This is a core building-block word combined with nouns to form possession (e.g. 'my book'); using the wrong pronoun breaks sentence generation. Every sibling possessive in this file ('Your'=Yako, 'His'=Yake, 'Mine'=Yangu, 'Ours'=Yetu...) correctly uses the possessive stem — this is the one glaring exception.
This means 'early morning', the opposite end of the day from 'Noon'. A user indicating midday would instead communicate early morning — a functionally serious error for scheduling/time communication.
'Mwanga' (light, a noun) followed directly by 'sana' (very) is not a grammatical descriptor — it lacks a verb/adjective. Sensory-overload words should be unambiguous.

'Pole' expresses sympathy for someone else's misfortune ('sorry to hear that'), not an apology for one's own action. 'Sorry' as a standalone social tile is typically used to apologize, for which 'Samahani' is correct (already used elsewhere for 'Excuse me').
Misspelled — missing 'h'. The real word is 'Kinafurahisha' (it is delightful).
Bare infinitive verb ('to be amazing') used where an exclamatory adjective is expected — non-idiomatic register for a reaction word.
Same issue as 'Wonderful' — bare infinitive verb form used as an exclamation, not idiomatic.
'Mstahimilivu' means 'patient/tolerant/long-suffering', not 'calm'. Wrong sense of a near-synonym.
Not a standard Swahili word — missing the 't'. Correct is 'Mtupu'.

Missing the object marker '-ni-' (me). As written it reads as 'it has exceeded ability' without specifying whose — ambiguous. Compare the correctly-formed sibling 'help-i-am-overwhelmed' = 'Imenizidi nguvu'.
Identical to the translation already used for 'Mouth' ('hb-mouth' = 'Mdomo'), collapsing two distinct body-part tiles into one word. The distinct plural form for lips is 'Midomo'.

'Kipigo' means 'a blow/strike' (from kupiga, to hit) — not 'joint'. Wrong word. The correct construction parallels 'Kifundo cha mguu' (ankle) / should-be 'Kifundo cha mkono' (wrist): 'Kifundo cha kidole'.
Misspelled — doubled 'm'. Correct spelling is 'Misuli'.
'Barafu' means 'ice', not 'snow'. Wrong sense of a related weather word — the correct word for snow is 'Theluji'.
'Kuna mtu' is a full existential clause ('there is a person / someone is here'), not a composable pronoun. As a core word meant to combine with other tiles it will not produce grammatical sentences.
'Nani' means 'Who', duplicating the separate 'Who' tile and losing the distinct possessive-question meaning of 'Whose'.
Translates to 'grain candy', recategorizing a granola bar as candy — a real food-category mismatch that matters if the tile is used to communicate dietary choices.
Two words ('this thing') for what should be a single composable core pronoun, adding unnecessary word-count cost for the AAC user versus a shorter form.
'Mwisho' is a noun ('the end'), inconsistent with sibling core-verbs in the same category that use bare verb stems (Anza, Maliza, Baki...). Part-of-speech mismatch within a verb tile set.

Inconsistent noun-class demonstrative choice versus the other core 'That' tile ('cw-that' = 'Ile'). Not wrong in isolation, but two different forms for the same core word risks confusing users learning the board.
Uses the class-6 plural subject prefix 'Ya-' ('they have sufficed me') without a specific plural referent. The generic, referent-free idiom uses class 9 agreement instead.

Wrong word entirely: চেষ্টা means 'attempt/try', not thirst. A thirsty user pressing this tile would say something meaningless ('[I] have received an attempt') instead of communicating a basic physiological need. The set already has the correct word elsewhere (fe-thirsty uses তৃষ্ণা পেয়েছে).

Broken conjunct corrupts the word. The intended term is জ্বালাপোড়া (burning/stinging sensation); as written it parses as জল ('water') + garbled remainder, producing a nonsensical or misleading symptom report in a health context.

স্বাগতম means 'Welcome' (as in greeting someone's arrival), not the conversational response to 'thank you'. Wrong sense of a polysemous concept — a speaker would sound like they're welcoming a guest, not acknowledging thanks.

Both 'Hand' (hb-hand) and 'Arm' (hb-arm) are translated identically as হাত, making it impossible for the AAC user to distinguish which body part is injured/hurting. In a health-body category used for injury/pain reporting, this ambiguity can materially delay accurate first aid or medical assessment.
findings.suggested: হাত (keep for Hand; give Arm its own word, see hb-arm)

findings.issue: Duplicate of hb-hand's translation. 'Arm' and 'Hand' become indistinguishable when spoken aloud, undermining precise injury/pain communication for a non-speaking user.

Essentially duplicates hb-heel's translation (গোড়ালি = heel). Bengali has a distinct standard word for ankle (টাখনু); as translated, a user reporting ankle pain would sound like they mean their heel, risking miscommunication about the injury site.

অনুশোচিত means 'remorseful/regretful', which is the emotion of guilt, not shame. The set already has a separate word for guilt (fe-guilty = দোষী), so this mistranslation conflates two distinct feelings a child needs to differentiate.
আদুরে লাগছে means 'feeling cute/pampered/spoiled', not 'feeling loved'. Wrong sense — an important affection/attachment word rendered as something closer to being fussed over.
গোলমাল means 'commotion/chaos/trouble', not the internal feeling of being mentally mixed-up/muddled. Wrong sense for an emotional-state word.
দুঃখিত is used in everyday speech primarily to mean 'sorry' (apology), not the standalone feeling of sadness. A child tapping this to express sadness risks sounding like they are apologizing instead.

শুনুন is the আপনি-level (formal) imperative, inconsistent with the তুমি-level honorific used throughout the rest of quick-talk (দাঁড়াও, এসো, কেমন আছো?, etc.). Honorific level must stay consistent across the set.
ঔষধ is the সাধু (literary) spelling. These strings must use চলিত (colloquial/spoken) register; the everyday spoken form is ওষুধ.

Ambiguous direction — reads as 'wanting to embrace [something/someone]' rather than 'wanting to be hugged'. Inconsistent with the directed-imperative pattern used for the same kind of physical-comfort request elsewhere in the set (help-hold-my-hand = আমার হাত ধরো).

Drops the first-person copula entirely (just the loanword 'ready' with no verb), inconsistent with the sibling pattern used two rows above for the same status-phrase type (help-i-am-okay = ঠিক আছি). Reads as a bare label rather than a first-person statement.
Same first-person-marking gap as help-i-am-ready; inconsistent with help-i-am-not-okay (ঠিক নেই).
নয় is a more formal/written negation form. চলিত (spoken) register calls for না.
Needlessly wordy (literally 'like [something worth] expressing thanks for') for a single-word feeling tile; costs the AAC user extra time per use and reads awkwardly rather than as a felt emotion.

Literally 'black mark/stain', which is ambiguous with a dirt stain or discoloration rather than clearly indicating a bruise from impact. The more specific and commonly understood colloquial term for bruise is not used.

Object marker কে should be suffixed directly to the noun (মাকে), as correctly done in help-call-my-mom (আমার মাকে ডাকো). Spacing it out is a script/orthography inconsistency across otherwise-identical constructions.
Same object-marker spacing inconsistency as help-i-need-my-mom.
Same object-marker spacing inconsistency as help-i-need-my-mom.
Retains the Latin acronym 'AAC' embedded in an otherwise Bengali sentence, violating the script rule (Bengali script throughout, no transliteration/Latin characters).

Verbal-noun form ('seeing'), inconsistent with sibling quick-chat root words in the same row that use imperative forms (qc_6 Go = যাও, qc_10 Put = রাখো, qc_11 Turn = ঘোরাও). Mixed forms make user-built sentences read unevenly.
Same verbal-noun vs. imperative inconsistency as ui:qc_7.
Same verbal-noun vs. imperative inconsistency as ui:qc_7.
